Analysis: [DOC monitoring system initialized. Ready to track healthcare costs as unavoidable, unpredictable consumer stress. Focus on OOP burden, medical debt, and care deferral.]

Description: Medical care CPI up 3.2% YoY in December 2025 (vs 2.9% in November). Medical care services index +3.5%, commodities +1.5%. Since 2000, medical care prices up 121.3% vs 86.1% general inflation.
Analysis: CONSISTENT WITH THESIS but MODERATING. Medical CPI at 3.2% is below ELEVATED threshold (>4%) but still exceeds general inflation (~2.9%). However, employers report actual costs rising 7-9% due to utilization and demand factors not captured in CPI. The gap between CPI and employer experience suggests CPI understates true burden.
Data Quote: Medical CPI 3.2% YoY; services 3.5%; 121.3% cumulative since 2000 vs 86.1% general
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — costs still exceed general inflation but moderating
Invalidation Criteria: If medical CPI drops below general CPI for 2+ quarters

Description: KFF 2025 Survey: Average deductible $1,886 (single), up 17% since 2020 and 43% over decade. Small firms: $2,631 avg deductible; 53% face $2,000+. 34% of all workers in plans with $2,000+ deductible. 72% face OOP max >$3,000.
Analysis: CONSISTENT WITH THESIS. Deductible burden continues rising — $1,886 average is above ELEVATED threshold. Small firm workers particularly stressed (53% face $2,000+). The 17% 5-year increase outpaces wage growth. OOP maximums approaching ACA limits ($9,450 individual). This creates "functionally underinsured" population.
Data Quote: Avg deductible $1,886 (+17% 5yr, +43% 10yr); small firms $2,631; 53% small firm workers $2,000+
CARL Relevance: High deductibles create barrier to care; force credit use
Invalidation Criteria: If avg deductible declines or grows slower than wages

Description: Commonwealth Fund 2024 survey: 23% of insured Americans are underinsured (high OOP costs relative to income). 57% of underinsured forgo needed care due to cost. 66% of underinsured have employer coverage.
Analysis: CRITICAL FINDING. Nearly 1 in 4 insured adults are underinsured — insurance card doesn't mean access. Majority (66%) have employer coverage, contradicting assumption that employer plans are adequate. 57% forgoing care means underinsurance is not just financial — it's creating health consequences. This validates DOC thesis on coverage inadequacy.
Data Quote: 23% underinsured; 57% forgo care; 66% have employer coverage
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — underinsurance is widespread even with employer coverage
Notes: Definition: OOP >10% of income OR deductible >5% of income

Description: CFPB: $88B medical debt in collections affecting 20% of Americans (1 in 5). 4.1% have medical debt on credit reports (9.7M consumers, down from 27M in 2022 due to credit bureau policy changes). KFF broader definition: 41% have medical/dental debt.
Analysis: CONSISTENT WITH THESIS. Medical debt remains massive problem — $88B in collections. The apparent improvement (27M → 9.7M on credit reports) is largely due to credit bureau changes removing small debts and paid debts, not actual reduction in debt burden. KFF's 41% broader rate shows true prevalence. CFPB rule to remove medical debt was VACATED July 2025.
Data Quote: $88B in collections; 20% affected; 4.1% on credit reports (down from 27M to 9.7M); 41% broader definition
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — medical debt remains widespread; policy protection removed
Invalidation Criteria: If medical debt in collections declines materially

Description: KFF 2025: 36% of adults skipped/postponed care due to cost. 18% said health worsened as result. Gallup 2025: 33% delayed/skipped care; 47% worried about affording healthcare next year (record high since 2021). 11% cannot access needed care.
Analysis: CONSISTENT WITH THESIS. Care deferral at 33-36% is above ELEVATED threshold (>30%) and approaching CRITICAL (>40%). Record-high anxiety (47%) about 2026 costs indicates worsening perception. 18% reporting worsened health is the amplifier — deferred care converts to acute events. The 11% unable to access is alarming for developed nation.
Data Quote: 36% skipped care; 18% health worsened; 47% worried about 2026 costs (record); 11% can't access
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — care deferral widespread and causing health consequences
CARL Relevance: Deferred care → worse health → higher eventual costs

Description: 20.2% reported cost-related medication non-adherence in 2022 survey. 12.9% delayed fills, 11.1% didn't fill, 7.9% skipped doses. Non-adherence causes $528B in morbidity/mortality costs annually; 100,000 preventable deaths; 25% of hospitalizations.
Analysis: CONSISTENT WITH THESIS. Non-adherence at 20% exceeds ELEVATED threshold. This is the care deferral cascade in action — cost barriers → skipped medication → worse outcomes → hospitalizations. The $528B annual cost and 100K preventable deaths show the human toll. Insulin, cardiovascular, and mental health meds are highest risk categories.
Data Quote: 20.2% non-adherence; 12.9% delayed fills; $528B annual cost; 100K preventable deaths; 25% of hospitalizations
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — medication non-adherence is widespread and deadly
CARL Relevance: Non-adherence leads to hospitalizations → medical debt

Description: IRA Medicare Drug Negotiation: First 10 drugs negotiated with 38-79% price reductions starting 2026. $2,000 annual Part D OOP cap effective 2025. $35/month insulin cap. 15 more drugs selected for 2027. CBO projects $98.5B Medicare savings over decade.
Analysis: POSITIVE DEVELOPMENT. IRA drug provisions are the most significant drug pricing reform in decades. The $2,000 cap and insulin limit provide immediate relief. However: (1) Only affects Medicare, not commercial; (2) Only 10 drugs initially; (3) Full savings take years to realize. This is partial thesis challenge for Rx segment but not invalidation.
Data Quote: 38-79% price cuts on 10 drugs; $2,000 OOP cap; $35 insulin; $98.5B projected savings
Thesis Impact: MIXED — positive policy intervention but limited scope
CARL Relevance: Reduces Rx burden for Medicare population only
Invalidation Criteria: If IRA provisions repealed or scope dramatically expanded
Notes: Applies to Medicare only; commercial unaffected

Description: Medical Care CPI rose to 3.4% YoY in February 2026 (BLS release March 11, 2026), up from 3.2% in January. Medical care services 3.5%. General CPI 2.4% — healthcare running 1pp above general inflation.
Analysis: RISING TREND. CPI acceleration (3.2%→3.4%) suggests upward momentum. Still below 4% ELEVATED threshold but trajectory matters. March 2026 data releases April 10, 2026. Gap vs employer-reported 9-10% actual cost growth confirms CPI understates burden.
Data Quote: Medical CPI 3.4% Feb 2026 vs 2.4% general CPI
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — costs still above general inflation and rising
CARL Relevance: Healthcare cost inflation exceeds wage growth → crowding out discretionary spending
Invalidation Criteria: If medical CPI drops to/below general CPI for 2+ consecutive months
Notes: March 2026 CPI data due April 10 — watch for continuation of rise

Description: ACA marketplace enrollment closed at 23.1M for 2026 — down 1.2M (-4.9%) from 2025 record of 24.3M. Enhanced subsidies expired Dec 31, 2025. March 2026 survey: 9% of prior ACA enrollees now uninsured. Avg subsidized enrollee premiums up 114%. Urban Institute: 4.8M total coverage loss in 2026.
Analysis: ACUTE 2026 TRIGGER. This is the single most important new development since Session 1. ACA subsidy lapse is creating a new wave of uninsured at exactly the moment CARL's other stress vectors are elevated. More than half of those who reenrolled are cutting food/food spending to afford premiums. Self-employed, gig workers, early retirees (55-64) disproportionately affected.
Data Quote: 23.1M enrolled 2026 (-4.9%); 9% of prior enrollees uninsured; premiums +114% avg; 4.8M projected uninsured [Urban Inst]
Source: CMS 2026 OEP; CNBC Mar 19 2026; KFF Jan 2026; Urban Institute
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — new acute trigger for care deferral and medical debt accumulation
CARL Relevance: ACA uninsured = zero coverage = deferred care → eventual acute medical debt event. Overlaps with CARL's consumer spending stress (cutting food to pay premiums).
Invalidation Criteria: If Congress reinstates enhanced subsidies retroactively
Notes: 67% of public says Congress did "wrong thing" not extending (KFF) — political motivation for reinstatement exists

Description: GLP-1 drug cost shock crystallizing for employers in 2025-2026. Employer GLP-1 costs up ~30%. 64% of large employers say "significant" impact on Rx spending. GLP-1 claims rose from 6.9% to 10.5% of total Rx claims (2023-2025). Employers project 11-12% Rx cost trend 2026. 1-in-5 large firms (200+ workers) now cover GLP-1 for weight loss; 43% of firms with 5,000+ workers.
Analysis: STRUCTURAL ESCALATION. GLP-1 is now the dominant driver of Rx cost trend. Universal coverage could push premiums 14% higher. Coverage decisions are creating new within-workforce access gaps (top earners at large firms get GLP-1 coverage; small firm workers and self-employed do not). Self-pay cost $349-499/mo is not accessible for bottom 60%. This is a new K-shape driver within healthcare itself.
Data Quote: GLP-1 employer costs +30%; claims 6.9%→10.5%; 64% large employers "significant"; 43% of 5,000+ firms covering
Source: KFF EHBS 2025; Mercer GLP-1 2026; PwC Behind the Numbers 2026
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — reinforces cost driver thesis; new K-shape within healthcare
CARL Relevance: GLP-1 costs pass through to all worker premiums even for those who don't use them; creates new healthcare cost wedge
Invalidation Criteria: If biosimilar competition drives GLP-1 prices below $100/mo (not before ~2032)
Notes: GLP-1 without competition until 2032+; structural cost driver for the thesis window

Description: Rural hospital financial crisis deepening. 182 total closures since 2010 (18 in past year). 46% of rural hospitals have negative operating margins. 432 rural hospitals at risk of closure. Medicaid non-expansion states: 53% rural hospitals in red, median margin -1.5%. Labor and delivery closures accelerating: 116 closures since 2020, 27 in 2025 alone. ACA subsidy lapse costing rural hospitals est. $1.6B in patient revenue.
Analysis: STRUCTURAL ACCELERATION. Rural hospital access crisis is compounding consumer healthcare stress. Rural communities (disproportionately lower-income) lose access, forcing longer travel times, delayed care, or no care at all. L&D closure surge is particularly acute — 116 closures means pregnant women in rural areas traveling 50+ miles to deliver. Medicare sequestration cut costs rural hospitals $509M/yr. Policy headwinds from ACA lapse + potential Medicaid cuts are compounding already-stressed margins.
Data Quote: 182 closures since 2010; 46% negative margin; 432 at risk; 116 L&D closures since 2020
Source: Chartis 2025 State of Rural Health; Fierce Healthcare; Commonwealth Fund Feb 2026
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — access crisis is structural; accelerating K-shape geography
CARL Relevance: Rural communities = disproportionately bottom 60% — this is access desert formation
Invalidation Criteria: If Rural Hospital Closure Relief Act (S.502) passes with meaningful funding
Notes: S.502 introduced but passage uncertain; Medicaid expansion in holdout states would help most

Description: KFF Health Tracking Poll Jan 2026: 66% of Americans worried about affording healthcare (top financial worry — above utilities, food, housing, gas). 55% say costs went up in past year; 56% expect costs to be less affordable next year. Paying for healthcare is now #1 financial worry. Care deferral 36%. ACA expiry directly cited as cause.
Analysis: RECORD STRESS LEVEL. 66% worried is a demand-level signal — behavioral changes are already happening before the credit data shows it. This is the leading indicator: worry → avoidance → deferred care → eventual medical event. 56% expecting worse affordability next year suggests more deferral and non-adherence loading in 2026. The worry level compounds CARL's "K-shape converging downward" thesis — healthcare worry now extends deeply into formerly secure cohorts.
Data Quote: 66% worried about healthcare affordability (Jan 2026 KFF poll); 55% say costs rose; 56% expect worse; #1 financial worry
Source: KFF Health Tracking Poll Jan 2026 (conducted Jan 13-20, 2026, n=1,426)
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — validates stress is at behavioral inflection point
CARL Relevance: Consumer financial worry at record = LEADING indicator of spending reduction and care avoidance; precedes credit data deterioration by 6-12 months
Invalidation Criteria: If major legislation reduces costs materially and anxiety drops below 50%
Notes: Congress showing no urgency on ACA subsidies per KFF poll analysis
